synopsis: The corpus uses the NTSB’s 2019 investigation of the 18 March 2018 Uber crash in Tempe as an on-road precedent: pedestrian detection occurred, but classification and path prediction were not correct in time [f10694]. Chapter 2 records that factory forward collision warning and AEB were disabled; Chapter 13 adds that shared radar frequencies were one reason for disabling factory AEB, according to a secondary summary [f1528, f11255]. The investigation also identified a design that precluded emergency braking in the relevant condition and relied on operator intervention; accounts describe a one-second action suppression, with emergency recognition 1.2 seconds before impact and braking beginning only 0.2 seconds before impact [f10695, f10697, f10698, f10871, f10872]. The lessons extend beyond algorithm performance to deficient safety risk management, oversight and safety culture, but the report was an automated-vehicle investigation, not a product-liability judgment [f10696, f11270, f10699]. Source attribution varies: some details are explicitly conveyed through secondary accounts, while parallel statements present the suppression and timing directly as NTSB findings [f10697, f10698, f10871, f10872, f11255].
